questions.commandDemand: Give the reason using the path of the current.
questions.stimulus: Two bulbs, A and B, are connected in a series circuit with one battery. Bulb A is removed from its holder, and bulb B goes out.
questions.stem: Explain why bulb B goes out when bulb A is removed.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the circuit is broken, so no current can flow
in a series circuit there is only one path for the current

chain.text: In a series circuit there is only one path for the current to flow.
Removing bulb A creates a gap, so the circuit is broken.
No current can flow through bulb B, so it goes out.

questions.modelAnswer: In a series circuit there is only one path for the current to flow around. When bulb A is removed there is a gap in that path, so the circuit is broken. No current can flow through the circuit, and therefore no current flows through bulb B, so bulb B goes out.
markPoints: In a series circuit there is only one path for the current
Removing bulb A breaks the circuit, so no current flows through B
questions.whyMarksLost: The words one path and broken circuit are the marks. 'The electricity cannot get through' describes it without using the circuit vocabulary.

questions.commandDemand: State the outcome and explain using the number of paths.
questions.stimulus: Two bulbs, C and D, are connected in a parallel circuit with one battery. Bulb C is removed from its holder.
questions.stem: Predict what happens to bulb D, and explain why.

fuzzyTraps.vague: D stays on because it is separate
fuzzyTraps.precise: D remains lit because it is on its own complete path for the current

chain.text: Bulb D remains lit.
In a parallel circuit each bulb is on its own separate path.
Removing C breaks only C's path; D's path is still complete, so current still flows through D.

questions.modelAnswer: Bulb D remains lit. In a parallel circuit each bulb is connected on its own separate path for the current. Removing bulb C breaks only the path that bulb C was on. The path through bulb D is still complete, so current can still flow through bulb D from the battery and it stays lit.
markPoints: Bulb D remains lit
Reason: in a parallel circuit each bulb is on its own separate complete path
questions.whyMarksLost: The word separate is what distinguishes parallel from series. Without it the answer does not explain why one break does not affect the other bulb.

questions.commandDemand: Read the table and identify the materials, quoting the evidence.
questions.stimulus:
Four materials were each placed in a gap in a circuit containing a bulb, and what happened was recorded.

Material 1: bulb lit brightly
Material 2: bulb did not light
Material 3: bulb lit brightly
Material 4: bulb did not light
questions.stem: Infer which materials are conductors of electricity and which are insulators. Explain how you decided.

fuzzyTraps.precise: 1 and 3 are conductors of electricity, because they allow current to flow and complete the circuit

chain.text: Materials 1 and 3 allowed the bulb to light.
They allowed current to flow, completing the circuit, so they are conductors of electricity.
Materials 2 and 4 did not allow current to flow, so the circuit stayed incomplete and they are insulators.

questions.modelAnswer: Materials 1 and 3 are conductors of electricity. When they were placed in the gap the bulb lit, which shows that current was able to flow through them and complete the circuit. Materials 2 and 4 are insulators. The bulb did not light with them in the gap, which shows that they did not allow current to flow, so the circuit remained incomplete.
markPoints: Materials 1 and 3 identified as conductors, with the lit bulb as evidence of current flowing
Materials 2 and 4 identified as insulators, with the unlit bulb as evidence
questions.whyMarksLost: The lit bulb is evidence, not the conclusion. State what the bulb lighting proves, which is that current flowed and the circuit was complete.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason using the effect on the current.
questions.stimulus: A circuit has one bulb and one battery, and the bulb lights brightly. A second identical battery is added in series, and the bulb becomes brighter.
questions.stem: Explain why the bulb becomes brighter.

fuzzyTraps.precise: more batteries increase the current flowing through the bulb

chain.text: Adding a second battery in series increases the electrical energy supplied to the circuit.
A larger current flows through the bulb.
More electrical energy is converted into light energy each second, so the bulb is brighter.

questions.modelAnswer: Adding a second battery in series increases the electrical energy supplied to the circuit, so a larger current flows through the bulb. With a larger current, more electrical energy is converted into light energy in the bulb each second, so the bulb glows more brightly.
markPoints: Adding a battery increases the current flowing through the bulb
More electrical energy is converted into light energy, so the bulb is brighter
questions.whyMarksLost: Power is an everyday word here. The mark scheme wants current, and the energy conversion in the bulb.

questions.commandDemand: Offer a workable circuit design and explain why it meets the requirement.
questions.stimulus: A designer wants a bedside lamp with two bulbs, so that if one bulb blows the other still works, and each bulb can be switched on independently.
questions.stem: Suggest how the bulbs and switches should be connected, and explain why your design meets both requirements.

fuzzyTraps.precise: connect the bulbs in parallel, each on its own path with its own switch

chain.text: Connect the two bulbs in parallel, each on its own branch.
Place a separate switch on each branch.
Each bulb has its own complete path, so a blown bulb or an open switch breaks only that branch.

questions.modelAnswer: The two bulbs should be connected in parallel, so that each bulb is on its own separate path from the battery, and a separate switch should be placed on each of those paths. If one bulb blows, only the path through that bulb is broken, and the other path is still complete so the second bulb still lights. Because each switch is on its own branch, opening one switch breaks only that branch, so each bulb can be switched on and off independently of the other.
markPoints: Bulbs connected in parallel, each on its own path
A separate switch on each branch
Explanation that breaking one branch leaves the other complete, meeting both requirements
questions.whyMarksLost: Two requirements are stated in the stem, so the explanation must answer both. Saying 'use parallel' answers the first and leaves the switch mark unclaimed.

questions.commandDemand: State what must be true for the circuit to work.
questions.stimulus: A student builds a circuit with a battery, a bulb and wires, but the bulb does not light. All the components are known to be working.
questions.stem: Describe two things the student should check.

fuzzyTraps.vague: check if it is plugged in properly
fuzzyTraps.precise: check that all connections are tight so that the circuit is complete

chain.text: Check that all the connections are tight and there is no gap in the circuit.
Check that the battery is the right way round and the bulb is screwed firmly into its holder.
The circuit must be complete for current to flow through the bulb.

questions.modelAnswer: The student should check that every connection is tight and that there is no gap anywhere in the circuit, because the circuit must be complete for a current to flow. The student should also check that the bulb is screwed firmly into its holder and that the wires are properly attached to both terminals of the battery, as a loose contact would leave the circuit incomplete and no current would flow through the bulb.
markPoints: Check that all connections are tight and there is no gap, so the circuit is complete
Check the bulb is firmly in its holder or the wires are attached to both battery terminals
questions.whyMarksLost: Both checks must come back to the same principle, that the circuit must be complete for current to flow. Listing checks with no reason is only half an answer.

questions.commandDemand: Give a similarity and a difference, referring to both circuits each time.
questions.stem: Compare a series circuit and a parallel circuit.

fuzzyTraps.precise: in a parallel circuit each bulb has its own separate path, so one break does not stop the others

chain.text: Both are complete circuits in which a current flows from the battery through the components.
A series circuit has only one path; a parallel circuit has separate paths for each component.
A break stops everything in a series circuit but only one branch in a parallel circuit.

questions.modelAnswer: Both a series circuit and a parallel circuit are complete circuits in which current flows from the battery through the components. However, a series circuit has only one path for the current, so all the components are on the same path, while a parallel circuit has separate paths for each component. As a result, a break anywhere in a series circuit stops the current everywhere, but a break in one branch of a parallel circuit leaves the other branches working.
markPoints: Similarity: both are complete circuits with current flowing from the battery
Difference: one path in series versus separate paths in parallel, with the consequence for a break
questions.whyMarksLost: Better and worse are not scientific comparisons. Describe the paths, and let the consequence follow from that.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason using the size of the food molecules.
questions.stem: Explain why food must be digested before the body can use it.

fuzzyTraps.vague: the body breaks it down to use it
fuzzyTraps.precise: digestion breaks large food molecules into smaller, soluble ones that can be absorbed

fuzzyTraps.vague: so it can go into the body
fuzzyTraps.precise: so it can pass through the wall of the small intestine into the bloodstream

chain.text: Food molecules such as starch and protein are too large to pass through the wall of the small intestine.
Digestion breaks them down into smaller, soluble substances.
These can be absorbed into the bloodstream and carried to the cells.

questions.modelAnswer: Food molecules such as starch and protein are too large to pass through the wall of the small intestine into the bloodstream. Digestion breaks these large molecules down into smaller, soluble substances. These smaller substances can then be absorbed through the wall of the small intestine into the bloodstream and carried to the cells of the body, where they are used.
markPoints: Large food molecules cannot pass through the wall of the small intestine
Digestion breaks them into smaller soluble substances that can be absorbed into the bloodstream
questions.whyMarksLost: The word absorbed and the destination, the bloodstream, are the marks. 'So the body can use it' names the purpose without the mechanism.

questions.commandDemand: Link the structure of the organ to its function.
questions.stimulus: The inner wall of the small intestine is covered with millions of tiny finger like projections.
questions.stem: Explain how these projections help the small intestine to carry out its function.

fuzzyTraps.precise: they increase the surface area for absorption

chain.text: The projections cover the inner wall of the small intestine.
They greatly increase the surface area of the inner wall.
More digested food can be absorbed into the bloodstream in the same amount of time.

questions.modelAnswer: The tiny finger like projections greatly increase the surface area of the inner wall of the small intestine. A larger surface area means that more digested food can come into contact with the wall at one time, so more digested food can be absorbed into the bloodstream in the same period. This makes absorption faster and more efficient.
markPoints: The projections increase the surface area of the inner wall
A larger surface area allows more digested food to be absorbed
questions.whyMarksLost: Surface area is the term, and absorption is the function. Any structure question of this kind is asking for the same pairing.

questions.commandDemand: State the path in order, naming each organ.
questions.stem: Describe the path taken by a piece of bread through the digestive system, naming what happens at each main stage.

fuzzyTraps.precise: it passes down the gullet into the stomach

chain.text: The bread is chewed into smaller pieces and mixed with saliva, which begins the digestion of starch.
It passes down the gullet to the stomach, where it is churned and digested further.
In the small intestine digestion is completed and the digested food is absorbed; water is absorbed in the large intestine.

questions.modelAnswer: In the mouth the bread is chewed into smaller pieces and mixed with saliva, which begins the digestion of starch. It then passes down the gullet into the stomach, where it is churned and digested further. It moves into the small intestine, where digestion is completed and the digested food is absorbed into the bloodstream. The undigested material passes into the large intestine, where water is absorbed, and the remainder is removed from the body.
markPoints: Mouth: chewed and mixed with saliva, starch digestion begins
Gullet to stomach, where food is churned and digested further
Small intestine: digestion completed and food absorbed; large intestine: water absorbed
questions.whyMarksLost: Listing the organs in order without saying what happens in each scores about one mark. The stem asks for both the path and the events.

questions.commandDemand: State the effect and explain it using the function of the missing part.
questions.stimulus: A patient has a large part of her small intestine removed in an operation.
questions.stem: Predict one effect this will have on her body, and explain why.

fuzzyTraps.precise: she cannot absorb as much digested food, because the surface area for absorption is reduced

chain.text: She will absorb less digested food, and may become weak or lose weight.
The small intestine is where digested food is absorbed into the bloodstream.
Removing part of it reduces the surface area available for absorption.

questions.modelAnswer: She will not be able to absorb as much digested food, and may lose weight or become weak. The small intestine is the organ where digested food is absorbed into the bloodstream. Removing a large part of it greatly reduces the surface area available for absorption, so less of the digested food passes into the bloodstream and more of it leaves the body unused.
markPoints: Less digested food is absorbed, leading to weight loss or weakness
Reason: the small intestine is the site of absorption, and the surface area is reduced
questions.whyMarksLost: Digestion and absorption are different processes. She can still digest; what she loses is the ability to absorb, and mixing the two loses the mark.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason using the action of the teeth and the surface area.
questions.stimulus: A student is told to chew his food thoroughly rather than swallowing it in large lumps.
questions.stem: Explain why chewing food thoroughly helps digestion.

fuzzyTraps.vague: small pieces are easier to swallow
fuzzyTraps.precise: smaller pieces have a larger total surface area for the digestive juices to act on

chain.text: Chewing breaks the food into smaller pieces.
Smaller pieces have a larger total surface area.
Digestive juices can act on more of the food at once, so digestion is faster.

questions.modelAnswer: Chewing breaks the food into much smaller pieces. Smaller pieces have a larger total surface area than one large lump of the same amount of food. This means the digestive juices can come into contact with more of the food at one time and act on it, so the food is digested more quickly and completely.
markPoints: Chewing breaks food into smaller pieces with a larger total surface area
Digestive juices can act on more of the food, so digestion is faster
questions.whyMarksLost: Easier swallowing is true but is not about digestion. The question asks about digestion, so the answer must reach the digestive juices.

questions.commandDemand: Read the results and state what they show about where digestion happens.
questions.stimulus:
Samples were taken from different parts of a person's digestive system two hours after a starchy meal, and tested for starch.

Mouth: starch present
Stomach: some starch present
Start of small intestine: trace of starch
End of small intestine: no starch
questions.stem: What can you infer from these results about the digestion of starch?

fuzzyTraps.precise: the starch was digested and broken down into smaller substances

chain.text: The amount of starch decreases along the digestive system and is absent by the end of the small intestine.
The starch is being digested and broken down into smaller substances as it travels.
The digestion of starch is completed by the time the food reaches the end of the small intestine.

questions.modelAnswer: The starch is gradually digested as the food travels through the digestive system. The amount of starch decreases from the mouth to the stomach and then to the start of the small intestine, and no starch remains at the end of the small intestine. This shows that starch is broken down into smaller substances along the way, and that its digestion is completed in the small intestine.
markPoints: Starch is digested and broken down progressively along the digestive system
Digestion of starch is completed in the small intestine, supported by the absence of starch at the end
questions.whyMarksLost: Saying the starch 'disappeared' or 'was absorbed' is wrong. Starch cannot be absorbed; it must first be broken down, and that distinction is the point of the question.

questions.commandDemand: Offer a fair method of testing and state what would be measured.
questions.stimulus: A student wants to find out whether saliva really does break down starch.
questions.stem: Suggest an experiment the student could carry out, including how the test would be made fair.

fuzzyTraps.vague: put saliva on starch and see
fuzzyTraps.precise: set up one tube with saliva and one without, and test both for starch after the same time

chain.text: Prepare two test tubes each containing the same amount of starch solution.
Add saliva to one tube and the same volume of water to the other.
Keep both at the same temperature for the same length of time.
Test both tubes for starch and compare the results.

questions.modelAnswer: The student should prepare two test tubes each containing the same amount of starch solution. Saliva should be added to the first tube and the same volume of water added to the second, which acts as the control. Both tubes should be kept at the same temperature for the same length of time. The student should then test the contents of both tubes for starch. If starch is present in the water tube but absent from the saliva tube, this shows that the saliva broke down the starch.
markPoints: Two setups, one with saliva and one without, as a control
Variables kept the same: amount of starch, temperature, time
Both tested for starch afterwards, with what the result would show
questions.whyMarksLost: The control tube is the mark most often missed. Without a tube that has no saliva, there is nothing to compare the result against.

questions.commandDemand: State the changes in order, naming the parts that move.
questions.stem: Describe what happens in the chest during inhalation.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the volume of the chest cavity increases
air flows into the lungs because the air pressure inside decreases

chain.text: The diaphragm contracts and moves downwards, and the rib muscles pull the ribcage upwards and outwards.
The volume of the chest cavity increases.
The air pressure inside the lungs decreases, so air flows in from outside.

questions.modelAnswer: During inhalation the diaphragm contracts and moves downwards, while the rib muscles contract to pull the ribcage upwards and outwards. These movements increase the volume of the chest cavity. As the volume increases, the air pressure inside the lungs decreases below the pressure outside the body, so air flows in through the nose and windpipe into the lungs.
markPoints: The diaphragm contracts and moves downwards
The ribcage moves upwards and outwards, increasing the volume of the chest cavity
Air pressure inside decreases, so air flows into the lungs
questions.whyMarksLost: Air is not sucked in. It flows in because the pressure inside becomes lower than outside, and the examiner wants that stated.

questions.commandDemand: Link the structure of the air sacs to their function.
questions.stimulus: The lungs contain millions of tiny air sacs, each surrounded by very fine blood vessels.
questions.stem: Explain how this structure helps gaseous exchange to take place efficiently.

fuzzyTraps.vague: the air sacs hold the air
fuzzyTraps.precise: the air sacs provide a large surface area for gaseous exchange

chain.text: Millions of tiny air sacs provide a very large total surface area.
Each is surrounded by fine blood vessels, so the gases have only a short distance to travel.
Oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out of it quickly.

questions.modelAnswer: The millions of tiny air sacs give the lungs a very large total surface area for gaseous exchange. Each air sac is surrounded by very fine blood vessels, so the gases only have to travel a very short distance between the air and the blood. Oxygen can therefore pass from the air in the sacs into the bloodstream, and carbon dioxide can pass from the blood into the air sacs, both very quickly and in large amounts.
markPoints: The air sacs provide a large surface area for gaseous exchange
Oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out, aided by the close blood vessels
questions.whyMarksLost: Both gases should be named, moving in opposite directions. Answers that mention only oxygen give half the exchange.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason using the body's need for oxygen.
questions.stimulus: A student's breathing rate is 16 breaths per minute at rest. After running for five minutes it rises to 34 breaths per minute.
questions.stem: Explain why the student's breathing rate increases during exercise.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the muscles need more oxygen for respiration to release more energy

fuzzyTraps.vague: to get rid of the bad air
fuzzyTraps.precise: to remove the carbon dioxide produced more quickly

chain.text: During exercise the muscles need more energy.
More energy is released by respiration, which requires more oxygen.
Breathing rate increases to take in more oxygen and remove the extra carbon dioxide produced.

questions.modelAnswer: During exercise the student's muscles are working harder and need more energy. This energy is released during respiration, which requires oxygen. The student therefore needs to take in more oxygen. Respiration also produces more carbon dioxide, which must be removed from the body. The breathing rate increases so that more oxygen can be taken into the lungs and more carbon dioxide can be removed, more quickly.
markPoints: Muscles need more energy during exercise
More energy is released by respiration, which requires more oxygen
More carbon dioxide is produced and must be removed more quickly
questions.whyMarksLost: Breathing and respiration are different. Breathing moves air; respiration releases energy inside the cells. Using them interchangeably costs marks.

questions.commandDemand: State the difference in composition, referring to both inhaled and exhaled air.
questions.stimulus:
The composition of inhaled and exhaled air was measured.

Inhaled air: 21 per cent oxygen, 0.04 per cent carbon dioxide
Exhaled air: 16 per cent oxygen, 4 per cent carbon dioxide
questions.stem: Compare inhaled and exhaled air, and explain the difference.

fuzzyTraps.precise: exhaled air contains less oxygen because some was absorbed into the blood

chain.text: Exhaled air contains less oxygen and much more carbon dioxide than inhaled air.
Some oxygen was absorbed into the bloodstream for respiration.
Carbon dioxide produced during respiration passed from the blood into the air sacs.

questions.modelAnswer: Exhaled air contains less oxygen than inhaled air, 16 per cent compared with 21 per cent, and much more carbon dioxide, 4 per cent compared with 0.04 per cent. This is because during gaseous exchange in the lungs some of the oxygen in the inhaled air passes into the bloodstream to be used in respiration, while carbon dioxide produced by respiration passes out of the blood into the air sacs and is breathed out.
markPoints: Exhaled air has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide, with figures quoted
Explained by gaseous exchange: oxygen absorbed into the blood, carbon dioxide released from it
questions.whyMarksLost: Note that exhaled air still contains 16 per cent oxygen. Writing that all the oxygen is used up contradicts the table in front of you.

questions.commandDemand: State the effect and explain using the function of the damaged part.
questions.stimulus: Smoking damages the walls of the air sacs in the lungs, causing many of them to break down and join into fewer, larger spaces.
questions.stem: Predict how this would affect the person, and explain why.

fuzzyTraps.vague: the lungs get damaged so breathing is hard
fuzzyTraps.precise: the surface area for gaseous exchange is reduced, so less oxygen enters the bloodstream

chain.text: The person will become breathless easily and be unable to exercise as before.
Fewer, larger spaces give a much smaller total surface area than many tiny air sacs.
Less oxygen can pass into the bloodstream, so the body cannot obtain the oxygen it needs.

questions.modelAnswer: The person will become breathless easily and will not be able to exercise as they did before. When the air sacs break down into fewer, larger spaces, the total surface area available for gaseous exchange is greatly reduced. Less oxygen can therefore pass from the lungs into the bloodstream with each breath, so the body cannot obtain enough oxygen for respiration, especially when the demand rises during exercise.
markPoints: The person becomes breathless or cannot exercise as well
Reason: reduced surface area for gaseous exchange, so less oxygen enters the bloodstream
questions.whyMarksLost: The link is through surface area, exactly as with the air sacs question. Any structure that is subdivided is there to increase surface area.

questions.commandDemand: Read the data and state what it shows about fitness.
questions.stimulus:
Two students ran the same distance. Their breathing rates were measured before, immediately after, and every minute during recovery.

Student A: 15 at rest, 32 immediately after, back to 15 after 3 minutes
Student B: 18 at rest, 40 immediately after, back to 18 after 8 minutes
questions.stem: Infer which student is fitter, and explain how the data supports your answer.

fuzzyTraps.vague: A breathes less so A is fitter
fuzzyTraps.precise: A's breathing rate returned to its resting value in a shorter time, showing a faster recovery

chain.text: Student A is fitter.
A's breathing rate rose less, from 15 to 32, compared with B's rise from 18 to 40.
A returned to the resting rate in 3 minutes while B took 8 minutes.

questions.modelAnswer: Student A is fitter. A's breathing rate rose by a smaller amount during the run, from 15 to 32 breaths per minute, while B's rose from 18 to 40. A's breathing rate also returned to its resting value in only 3 minutes, whereas B took 8 minutes. A shorter recovery time shows that Student A's body was able to supply the oxygen needed and return to normal more quickly.
markPoints: Student A identified as fitter
Both the smaller rise and the shorter recovery time quoted as evidence
questions.whyMarksLost: Recovery time is the stronger evidence and is worth a mark on its own. Comparing only the peak rates uses half the table.

questions.commandDemand: Offer a method and state what result would prove the point.
questions.stimulus: A student claims that exhaled air contains more carbon dioxide than inhaled air.
questions.stem: Suggest how the student could test this claim, and state what result would support it.

fuzzyTraps.precise: bubble exhaled air through limewater, which turns milky in the presence of carbon dioxide

chain.text: Bubble exhaled air through one tube of limewater and ordinary air through an identical tube.
Limewater turns milky in the presence of carbon dioxide.
If the exhaled air tube turns milky faster, exhaled air contains more carbon dioxide.

questions.modelAnswer: The student should bubble exhaled air through a test tube of limewater, and bubble the same volume of ordinary air through an identical test tube of limewater for comparison. Limewater turns milky in the presence of carbon dioxide. If the limewater through which the exhaled air was bubbled turns milky more quickly or more strongly than the other, this supports the claim that exhaled air contains more carbon dioxide than inhaled air.
markPoints: Bubble exhaled air through limewater, with ordinary air as a comparison
Result stated: the exhaled air tube turns the limewater milky faster
questions.whyMarksLost: Without the comparison tube the test shows only that exhaled air contains carbon dioxide, not that it contains more, which is what the claim says.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason using what the two sides of the heart carry.
questions.stimulus: The human heart is divided into a left side and a right side by a thick wall, with no opening between them.
questions.stem: Explain why it is important that the two sides of the heart are kept separate.

fuzzyTraps.vague: so the blood does not get mixed up
fuzzyTraps.precise: so that oxygenated and deoxygenated blood do not mix
oxygen rich and oxygen poor blood

chain.text: The right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs; the left side pumps oxygenated blood to the body.
The wall prevents the two from mixing.
Blood reaching the body carries as much oxygen as possible, so the cells receive enough oxygen.

questions.modelAnswer: The right side of the heart pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs to take in oxygen, while the left side pumps oxygenated blood from the lungs to the rest of the body. The thick wall keeps the two apart so that oxygenated and deoxygenated blood do not mix. This means the blood sent to the body carries as much oxygen as possible, so the cells receive all the oxygen they need for respiration.
markPoints: The right side carries deoxygenated blood and the left side oxygenated blood
Keeping them separate prevents mixing, so blood to the body carries maximum oxygen
questions.whyMarksLost: Clean and dirty are not scientific terms and score nothing. Oxygenated and deoxygenated are the words the mark scheme uses.

questions.commandDemand: State the path in order, naming the organs.
questions.stem: Describe the path taken by a drop of blood as it travels from the lungs to a muscle in the leg and back to the heart.

fuzzyTraps.vague: the blood goes round the body
fuzzyTraps.precise: the blood travels from the lungs to the heart, then is pumped to the leg muscle

chain.text: Oxygenated blood travels from the lungs to the left side of the heart.
The heart pumps it through blood vessels to the muscle in the leg.
Oxygen is given to the muscle cells, and the now deoxygenated blood returns to the right side of the heart.

questions.modelAnswer: Oxygenated blood leaves the lungs and travels to the left side of the heart. The heart pumps this blood through blood vessels to the muscle in the leg. At the muscle, oxygen and digested food pass from the blood to the muscle cells, and carbon dioxide passes from the cells into the blood. The blood, now deoxygenated, then travels back through blood vessels to the right side of the heart.
markPoints: Oxygenated blood travels from the lungs to the heart
The heart pumps it to the leg muscle, where oxygen is delivered to the cells
Deoxygenated blood returns to the heart
questions.whyMarksLost: The blood passes through the heart between the lungs and the leg. Answers that send it straight from lungs to leg lose the mark for the heart's role as a pump.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason using the demand of the muscles.
questions.stimulus: A student's heart rate is 72 beats per minute at rest and 145 beats per minute during exercise.
questions.stem: Explain why the heart rate increases during exercise.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the heart beats faster to pump blood around the body more quickly

chain.text: The muscles need more oxygen and digested food to release more energy by respiration.
The heart beats faster to pump blood around the body more quickly.
Oxygen and food are delivered to the muscles faster, and carbon dioxide is removed faster.

questions.modelAnswer: During exercise the muscles are working harder and need more energy, which is released during respiration. Respiration requires oxygen and digested food, so the muscles need these to be delivered more quickly. The heart therefore beats faster to pump blood around the body more rapidly, so that more oxygen and digested food reach the muscles and the carbon dioxide produced is carried away more quickly.
markPoints: Muscles need more oxygen and digested food for respiration to release energy
A faster heart rate delivers these more quickly and removes carbon dioxide faster
questions.whyMarksLost: 'The heart works harder' repeats the observation. The mark is for what the blood is delivering and why it is needed faster.

questions.commandDemand: State the effect and explain using the function of blood.
questions.stimulus: A person has a condition in which their blood carries much less oxygen than normal.
questions.stem: Predict how this would affect the person during exercise, and explain why.

fuzzyTraps.precise: less oxygen reaches the muscles, so less energy is released by respiration

chain.text: The person will tire quickly and be unable to exercise for long.
Less oxygen is carried to the muscle cells.
Less energy can be released by respiration in the muscles.

questions.modelAnswer: The person will become tired very quickly and will not be able to exercise for long. Because their blood carries less oxygen, less oxygen is delivered to the muscle cells. Respiration in the muscles requires oxygen to release energy, so with less oxygen available less energy can be released. The muscles therefore cannot work as hard or for as long.
markPoints: The person tires quickly or cannot exercise for long
Reason: less oxygen reaches the muscles, so less energy is released by respiration
questions.whyMarksLost: The chain must reach energy. Stopping at 'less oxygen' does not explain why that makes the person tired.

questions.commandDemand: Link the two systems and say how they work together.
questions.stem: Explain how the respiratory system and the circulatory system work together to supply oxygen to a muscle.

fuzzyTraps.vague: the lungs give oxygen to the blood
fuzzyTraps.precise: oxygen passes from the air sacs into the bloodstream during gaseous exchange

chain.text: Air is breathed into the lungs and oxygen passes from the air sacs into the blood during gaseous exchange.
The oxygenated blood travels to the heart, which pumps it around the body.
The blood carries the oxygen to the muscle, where it passes into the cells for respiration.

questions.modelAnswer: The respiratory system brings air into the lungs, where oxygen passes from the air sacs into the bloodstream during gaseous exchange. This oxygenated blood then travels to the heart, which is part of the circulatory system. The heart pumps the oxygenated blood through blood vessels to all parts of the body, including the muscle. At the muscle, the oxygen passes from the blood into the muscle cells, where it is used in respiration to release energy.
markPoints: Oxygen enters the blood from the air sacs during gaseous exchange in the lungs
The heart pumps the oxygenated blood through blood vessels around the body
Oxygen passes from the blood into the muscle cells for respiration
questions.whyMarksLost: This is a synoptic question and the marks are spread across both systems. An answer that stays inside one system can only earn part of them.

questions.commandDemand: Read the data and identify the vessel, giving the evidence.
questions.stimulus:
Blood samples were taken from three blood vessels and the amount of oxygen in each was measured.

Vessel X: high oxygen, leaving the lungs
Vessel Y: low oxygen, entering the lungs
Vessel Z: low oxygen, leaving a leg muscle
questions.stem: Infer why Vessel Z contains blood with a low amount of oxygen. Explain your reasoning.

fuzzyTraps.vague: the leg used up the oxygen
fuzzyTraps.precise: the muscle cells absorbed oxygen from the blood for respiration

chain.text: Vessel Z carries blood away from the leg muscle and its oxygen content is low.
The muscle cells absorbed oxygen from the blood as it passed through.
The oxygen was used in respiration to release energy for the muscle to work.

questions.modelAnswer: Vessel Z carries blood away from the leg muscle. As the blood passed through the muscle, oxygen passed from the blood into the muscle cells. The muscle cells used this oxygen in respiration to release the energy needed for the muscle to work. The blood leaving the muscle is therefore deoxygenated and contains a low amount of oxygen.
markPoints: Oxygen passed from the blood into the muscle cells
The oxygen was used in respiration to release energy
questions.whyMarksLost: 'Used up the oxygen' is close but vague. Naming respiration and energy is what turns the observation into an explanation.

questions.commandDemand: Offer a practical action and explain the benefit to the system.
questions.stimulus: A doctor advises a patient to exercise regularly to improve the health of the heart.
questions.stem: Suggest how regular exercise benefits the circulatory system, and explain why.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the heart is a muscle, and regular exercise makes it stronger

chain.text: The heart becomes stronger with regular exercise.
The heart is a muscle, and like other muscles it becomes stronger when it is used regularly.
A stronger heart pumps more blood with each beat, so oxygen and food are delivered more efficiently.

questions.modelAnswer: Regular exercise makes the heart stronger. The heart is a muscle, and like any other muscle it becomes stronger when it is worked regularly. A stronger heart can pump a larger volume of blood with each beat, so oxygen and digested food are delivered to the body more efficiently and the resting heart rate can be lower.
markPoints: The heart is a muscle and becomes stronger with regular exercise
A stronger heart pumps blood more efficiently, delivering oxygen and food better
questions.whyMarksLost: The mark depends on recognising the heart as a muscle. Without that, there is no mechanism for why exercise would help it.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason using photosynthesis and what the plant needs.
questions.stimulus: Plant A is left on a sunny windowsill. Plant B is placed in a dark cupboard. Both are watered equally. After three days Plant A has grown taller than Plant B.
questions.stem: Explain why Plant A grew taller than Plant B.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the plant needs sunlight to carry out photosynthesis and make food

fuzzyTraps.vague: it makes energy from the sun
fuzzyTraps.precise: it makes food, which stores the energy the plant needs for growth

chain.text: Plant A received sunlight while Plant B did not.
Plant A could carry out photosynthesis, using sunlight to make food.
Plant B could not photosynthesise and had no food supply for growth.

questions.modelAnswer: Plant A received sunlight, so it was able to carry out photosynthesis. During photosynthesis the plant uses sunlight, absorbed by the chlorophyll in its leaves, to make food. This food provides what the plant needs to grow. Plant B was kept in the dark and had no sunlight, so it could not carry out photosynthesis and could not make food, and therefore it could not grow as tall.
markPoints: Plant A had sunlight so could carry out photosynthesis and make food
Plant B had no sunlight, so it could not photosynthesise or make food for growth
questions.whyMarksLost: Plants make food, not energy. Writing that the plant 'makes energy from the sun' is marked wrong even though the idea is close.

questions.commandDemand: State what goes in and what comes out, naming all four.
questions.stem: Describe what a plant needs for photosynthesis and what it produces.

fuzzyTraps.precise: it needs sunlight, water and carbon dioxide, and it needs chlorophyll to absorb the light

chain.text: The plant needs carbon dioxide, water and sunlight.
It also needs chlorophyll in its leaves to absorb the sunlight.
It produces food, which is stored, and oxygen, which is released.

questions.modelAnswer: For photosynthesis a plant needs carbon dioxide from the air, water from the soil, and sunlight. It also needs chlorophyll, the green substance in its leaves, to absorb the sunlight. Using these, the plant produces food, which it uses for growth or stores, and oxygen, which is released into the air.
markPoints: Inputs named: carbon dioxide, water, sunlight, with chlorophyll needed to absorb the light
Outputs named: food and oxygen
questions.whyMarksLost: Chlorophyll is a requirement, not an input that gets used up. Oxygen as a product is the half most often forgotten.

questions.commandDemand: Link the structure of the leaf to photosynthesis.
questions.stimulus: Most leaves are broad, flat and thin, and are arranged so that they do not overlap each other.
questions.stem: Explain how these features help the leaf carry out photosynthesis.

fuzzyTraps.precise: a large surface area allows the leaf to absorb more sunlight

chain.text: Broad and flat leaves have a large surface area.
This allows more sunlight to be absorbed for photosynthesis.
Not overlapping means each leaf receives sunlight rather than being shaded by another.

questions.modelAnswer: Broad and flat leaves have a large surface area, which allows them to absorb more sunlight for photosynthesis. Being thin means that carbon dioxide does not have far to travel to reach the cells inside. Arranging the leaves so that they do not overlap ensures that each leaf is exposed to sunlight rather than being shaded by the leaves above it, so more of the plant's leaves can photosynthesise.
markPoints: Large surface area to absorb more sunlight for photosynthesis
Non overlapping arrangement so leaves are not shaded and each receives sunlight
questions.whyMarksLost: The stem gives three features and expects at least two to be explained. Answering only about size claims one mark of two.

questions.commandDemand: Read the results and state which factor is needed, comparing the right pair.
questions.stimulus:
Four identical potted plants were kept for a week and then their leaves tested for starch.

Plant 1, in sunlight, watered, normal air: starch present
Plant 2, in darkness, watered, normal air: no starch
Plant 3, in sunlight, watered, air with carbon dioxide removed: no starch
Plant 4, in sunlight, not watered, normal air: no starch
questions.stem: What can you infer from these results? Explain how the data supports each conclusion.

fuzzyTraps.vague: plants need everything to make starch
fuzzyTraps.precise: sunlight, carbon dioxide and water are each needed for photosynthesis

chain.text: Comparing Plant 1 with Plant 2, only the light differed, and only the lit plant made starch.
Comparing Plant 1 with Plant 3, only the carbon dioxide differed, and only the plant with it made starch.
Comparing Plant 1 with Plant 4, only the water differed, and only the watered plant made starch.

questions.modelAnswer: Sunlight, carbon dioxide and water are all needed for photosynthesis. Comparing Plant 1 with Plant 2, where only the light differed, only the plant in sunlight produced starch, so sunlight is needed. Comparing Plant 1 with Plant 3, where only the carbon dioxide differed, only the plant supplied with carbon dioxide produced starch, so carbon dioxide is needed. Comparing Plant 1 with Plant 4, where only the water differed, only the watered plant produced starch, so water is needed.
markPoints: Sunlight is needed, supported by comparing Plants 1 and 2
Carbon dioxide is needed, supported by comparing Plants 1 and 3
Water is needed, supported by comparing Plants 1 and 4
questions.whyMarksLost: Each conclusion needs its own named pair. Writing 'the results show plants need all three' without the comparisons earns one mark of three.

questions.commandDemand: State the outcome and explain using photosynthesis.
questions.stimulus: A student covers part of a leaf on a living plant with black paper and leaves the plant in sunlight for two days. The leaf is then tested for starch.
questions.stem: Predict the result of the starch test on the covered and uncovered parts, and explain why.

fuzzyTraps.vague: the covered part will be white
fuzzyTraps.precise: the covered part will show no starch, so it will not turn blue black in the test

chain.text: The uncovered part received sunlight, so it could photosynthesise and make starch.
The covered part received no sunlight, so it could not photosynthesise.
Starch is present only in the uncovered part.

questions.modelAnswer: The uncovered part of the leaf will show that starch is present, while the covered part will show no starch. The uncovered part received sunlight, so it was able to carry out photosynthesis and produce food, which was stored as starch. The black paper blocked the sunlight from reaching the covered part, so photosynthesis could not take place there and no starch was produced.
markPoints: Starch present in the uncovered part and absent in the covered part
Reason: sunlight is needed for photosynthesis, and the paper blocked it
questions.whyMarksLost: Both regions must be predicted. Answering only about the covered part leaves the comparison, which is the point of the experiment, incomplete.

questions.commandDemand: Offer a workable change and explain the effect on photosynthesis.
questions.stimulus: A farmer grows lettuce inside a greenhouse and wants the plants to grow faster.
questions.stem: Suggest one change the farmer could make, and explain how it would help the plants grow faster.

fuzzyTraps.vague: give them more light so they grow
fuzzyTraps.precise: more light increases the rate of photosynthesis, so more food is made for growth

chain.text: Provide extra lighting inside the greenhouse, or increase the carbon dioxide supply.
This increases the rate of photosynthesis.
The plants make more food, so they grow faster.

questions.modelAnswer: The farmer could install extra lamps to provide more light inside the greenhouse. More light increases the rate of photosynthesis in the lettuce leaves, so the plants can make more food in the same amount of time. With more food available for growth, the lettuce plants grow faster.
markPoints: A workable change such as more light, more carbon dioxide, or a warmer temperature
Explained as increasing the rate of photosynthesis, so more food is made for growth
questions.whyMarksLost: The phrase rate of photosynthesis is what makes this an explanation. 'More light is better for plants' is an assertion.

questions.commandDemand: Give a similarity and a difference, referring to both processes each time.
questions.stem: Compare photosynthesis and respiration in a green plant.

fuzzyTraps.vague: plants photosynthesise in the day and respire at night
fuzzyTraps.precise: plants respire at all times, while photosynthesis only occurs when there is light

chain.text: Both take place in the cells of the plant and both involve oxygen and carbon dioxide.
Photosynthesis makes food and uses carbon dioxide, releasing oxygen.
Respiration breaks down food to release energy, using oxygen and releasing carbon dioxide.

questions.modelAnswer: Both photosynthesis and respiration take place inside the cells of a green plant, and both involve oxygen and carbon dioxide. However, photosynthesis makes food using carbon dioxide, water and sunlight, and releases oxygen, while respiration breaks down food to release energy, using oxygen and releasing carbon dioxide. Photosynthesis takes place only when there is light, whereas respiration takes place at all times, both day and night.
markPoints: Similarity: both occur in the plant's cells and both involve oxygen and carbon dioxide
Difference: photosynthesis makes food and releases oxygen; respiration breaks down food and releases carbon dioxide
Difference in timing: photosynthesis needs light, respiration occurs at all times
questions.whyMarksLost: A very common error is writing that plants respire only at night. They respire constantly; at night respiration is simply the only one of the two happening.

questions.commandDemand: State the levels in order from smallest to largest.
questions.stem: Describe how cells are organised to form a body system.

fuzzyTraps.precise: similar cells form a tissue, tissues form an organ, and organs form a system

chain.text: Similar cells that carry out the same function group together to form a tissue.
Different tissues working together form an organ.
Several organs working together form a body system.

questions.modelAnswer: Cells are the smallest unit of a living thing. Many similar cells that carry out the same function group together to form a tissue. Different tissues working together form an organ, such as the heart or the stomach. Several organs that work together to carry out a particular function form a body system, such as the circulatory system.
markPoints: Similar cells form a tissue, and tissues form an organ
Organs working together form a body system
questions.whyMarksLost: The order is the answer. Naming the four words without saying how each level builds from the one below does not show the organisation.

questions.commandDemand: Give a similarity and a difference, referring to both cell types each time.
questions.stem: Compare a plant cell with an animal cell.

fuzzyTraps.precise: plant cells contain chloroplasts, which animal cells do not

chain.text: Both have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus.
A plant cell has a cell wall outside the membrane; an animal cell does not.
A plant cell may contain chloroplasts; an animal cell never does.

questions.modelAnswer: Both plant cells and animal cells have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus. However, a plant cell also has a cell wall outside its cell membrane, which gives the cell a fixed shape, while an animal cell has no cell wall. A plant cell may also contain chloroplasts for photosynthesis, which animal cells never have.
markPoints: Similarity: both have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and nucleus
Difference: plant cells have a cell wall and may have chloroplasts, which animal cells lack
questions.whyMarksLost: Cell wall and cell membrane are different structures. Plant cells have both; animal cells have only the membrane, and confusing the two loses the mark.

questions.commandDemand: Link the structure of the cell to the job it does.
questions.stimulus: A root hair cell has a long thin extension that projects out into the soil.
questions.stem: Explain how this shape helps the root hair cell carry out its function.

fuzzyTraps.vague: it reaches into the soil to get water
fuzzyTraps.precise: the extension increases the surface area for absorbing water and mineral salts

chain.text: The long thin extension projects out into the soil.
This greatly increases the surface area of the cell in contact with the soil.
More water and mineral salts can be absorbed from the soil.

questions.modelAnswer: The long thin extension greatly increases the surface area of the root hair cell that is in contact with the soil. A larger surface area means that more water and mineral salts can be absorbed from the soil at the same time, so the plant can take up what it needs more quickly and efficiently.
markPoints: The extension increases the surface area in contact with the soil
More water and mineral salts can be absorbed
questions.whyMarksLost: Mineral salts should be named alongside water. Roots absorb both, and mentioning only water is an incomplete answer.

questions.commandDemand: Link the structure of the cell to the job it does.
questions.stimulus: A red blood cell has no nucleus and is shaped like a disc that is pushed in on both sides.
questions.stem: Explain how these features help the red blood cell carry out its function.

fuzzyTraps.vague: it is a good shape for blood
fuzzyTraps.precise: the shape gives a larger surface area for absorbing oxygen

chain.text: Having no nucleus leaves more space inside the cell.
More oxygen can be carried by each cell.
The disc shape pushed in on both sides gives a larger surface area.
Oxygen can be absorbed and released more quickly.

questions.modelAnswer: Having no nucleus leaves more space inside the red blood cell, so each cell can carry a larger amount of oxygen. The disc shape that is pushed in on both sides gives the cell a larger surface area for its size, so oxygen can pass into and out of the cell more quickly. Together these features allow the cell to transport oxygen around the body efficiently.
markPoints: No nucleus means more space to carry oxygen
The shape increases surface area, so oxygen is absorbed and released more quickly
questions.whyMarksLost: Two features are given in the stem, so two benefits are expected. Explaining only the shape claims one of the two marks.

questions.commandDemand: Read the description and identify the cell type, giving the evidence.
questions.stimulus:
Three cells were viewed under a microscope.

Cell P: has a cell wall, chloroplasts, and a large space in the middle
Cell Q: no cell wall, disc shaped, no nucleus
Cell R: no cell wall, has a nucleus, has a long thin extension carrying messages
questions.stem: Infer what each cell is, and give the evidence you used.

fuzzyTraps.vague: Q is a blood cell because it is round
fuzzyTraps.precise: Q is a red blood cell because it is disc shaped and has no nucleus

chain.text: A cell wall and chloroplasts mean P is a plant cell.
Disc shaped with no nucleus means Q is a red blood cell.
A long thin extension that carries messages means R is a nerve cell.

questions.modelAnswer: Cell P is a plant cell, because it has a cell wall and chloroplasts, which only plant cells have. Cell Q is a red blood cell, because it is disc shaped and has no nucleus, which are the features of a red blood cell. Cell R is a nerve cell, because it has a long thin extension that carries messages from one part of the body to another.
markPoints: All three cells correctly identified
Each identification supported by the distinguishing feature from the description
questions.whyMarksLost: The evidence must be the feature that only that cell has. Chloroplasts identify a plant cell; simply being green would not.

questions.commandDemand: State the effect and explain using the function of the missing structure.
questions.stimulus: A plant cell is treated so that its chloroplasts stop working, although the rest of the cell is unharmed.
questions.stem: Predict what will happen to the plant, and explain why.

fuzzyTraps.vague: the plant will die because it is damaged
fuzzyTraps.precise: the plant cannot photosynthesise, so it cannot make food and will eventually die

chain.text: The plant will stop growing and eventually die.
Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which absorbs sunlight for photosynthesis.
Without working chloroplasts the plant cannot photosynthesise or make food.

questions.modelAnswer: The plant will stop growing and will eventually die. Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which absorbs the sunlight needed for photosynthesis. If the chloroplasts stop working, the plant can no longer carry out photosynthesis and cannot make its own food. Without a supply of food the plant has nothing to use for growth and cannot survive.
markPoints: The plant stops growing and eventually dies
Reason: without working chloroplasts it cannot photosynthesise or make food
questions.whyMarksLost: The chain from chloroplast to chlorophyll to photosynthesis to food is what earns the second mark. Skipping to 'it dies' gives only the prediction.

questions.commandDemand: Offer a reason and explain it using the idea of specialisation.
questions.stimulus: The human body contains many different types of cell, each with a different shape and structure.
questions.stem: Suggest why the body has many different types of cell rather than one type.

fuzzyTraps.precise: each type of cell is specialised, with a structure suited to its particular function

chain.text: Each type of cell is specialised to carry out a particular function.
Its structure is suited to that function, such as a red blood cell's shape for carrying oxygen.
Each job is carried out more efficiently than a single general cell could manage.

questions.modelAnswer: Each type of cell is specialised to carry out a particular function, and its structure is suited to that function. For example, a red blood cell has no nucleus so it can carry more oxygen, while a root hair cell has a long extension to absorb water. Because each cell type is built for its own job, that job is carried out far more efficiently than it would be by a single general purpose cell.
markPoints: Each cell type is specialised for a particular function
Its structure is suited to that function, so the job is done more efficiently
questions.whyMarksLost: The word specialised, and the link between structure and function, are what the mark scheme rewards. An example helps but does not replace the principle.

questions.commandDemand: State the process in order using the correct terms.
questions.stem: Describe what happens during fertilisation in humans.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the nucleus of the sperm fuses with the nucleus of the egg

chain.text: A sperm reaches the egg in the oviduct.
The nucleus of the sperm fuses with the nucleus of the egg.
This forms a single cell, which then divides and develops.

questions.modelAnswer: During fertilisation a sperm reaches the egg. The nucleus of the sperm then fuses with the nucleus of the egg to form a single cell. This fertilised egg then divides repeatedly and develops into an embryo, which grows in the uterus.
markPoints: The sperm and egg meet, and their nuclei fuse
A fertilised egg is formed, which develops into an embryo
questions.whyMarksLost: Fuse is the mark word. 'The sperm goes into the egg' describes the approach but not the event that defines fertilisation.

questions.commandDemand: Link the structure to how it supports the developing baby.
questions.stimulus: A developing baby in the uterus is connected to the mother by the umbilical cord.
questions.stem: Explain the function of the umbilical cord.

fuzzyTraps.precise: it carries digested food and oxygen from the mother to the developing baby

chain.text: It carries oxygen and digested food from the mother to the developing baby.
It carries waste, including carbon dioxide, away from the baby to the mother.
The baby cannot eat or breathe for itself while in the uterus.

questions.modelAnswer: The umbilical cord carries oxygen and digested food from the mother's blood to the developing baby, which the baby needs for respiration and growth. It also carries waste substances, including carbon dioxide, away from the baby to the mother, so that she can remove them. This is necessary because the developing baby cannot eat or breathe for itself while it is in the uterus.
markPoints: Carries oxygen and digested food from the mother to the baby
Carries waste products, including carbon dioxide, from the baby to the mother
questions.whyMarksLost: The traffic goes both ways. Answers that mention only the food coming in claim one of the two marks.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason using what the developing baby needs.
questions.stimulus: A pregnant woman is advised to eat a balanced diet with plenty of nutrients, and to avoid smoking.
questions.stem: Explain why this advice is important for the developing baby.

fuzzyTraps.vague: smoking is bad for the baby
fuzzyTraps.precise: harmful substances from smoking pass to the baby through the umbilical cord

chain.text: The baby obtains all its nutrients from the mother, and needs them for growth and development.
Harmful substances from cigarette smoke can pass from the mother's blood to the baby.
These reduce the oxygen the baby receives and can harm its development.

questions.modelAnswer: The developing baby obtains all of its nutrients from the mother through the umbilical cord, so the mother must eat a balanced diet to supply the nutrients the baby needs for growth and development. If the mother smokes, harmful substances from the cigarette smoke can pass from her blood into the baby's blood. These reduce the amount of oxygen the baby receives and can harm its growth and development.
markPoints: The baby obtains its nutrients from the mother and needs them for growth
Harmful substances from smoking pass to the baby and reduce oxygen or harm development
questions.whyMarksLost: Both halves of the advice are in the stem, so both need answering. The route, through the umbilical cord, is what makes it an explanation.

questions.commandDemand: Give a similarity and a difference, referring to both cells each time.
questions.stem: Compare the sperm cell and the egg cell.

fuzzyTraps.vague: the sperm is small and the egg is big
fuzzyTraps.precise: the egg is larger because it contains a store of food for the developing embryo

chain.text: Both are sex cells and both contain a nucleus that fuses at fertilisation.
The sperm has a tail so it can swim towards the egg.
The egg is much larger and contains a store of food for the developing embryo.

questions.modelAnswer: Both the sperm cell and the egg cell are sex cells, and both contain a nucleus which fuses with the other at fertilisation. However, the sperm cell has a tail which allows it to swim towards the egg, while the egg cell has no tail and cannot move by itself. The egg cell is also much larger than the sperm cell, because it contains a store of food to nourish the embryo after fertilisation.
markPoints: Similarity: both are sex cells containing a nucleus that fuses at fertilisation
Difference: the sperm has a tail for swimming, while the larger egg carries a food store
questions.whyMarksLost: Size alone is a weak difference. The reason for the size, the food store, is what earns the mark.

questions.commandDemand: Read the data and state what it shows about development.
questions.stimulus:
The mass of a developing baby was recorded during pregnancy.

End of month 3: 25 g
End of month 5: 300 g
End of month 7: 1200 g
End of month 9: 3400 g
questions.stem: What can you infer about the growth of the baby during pregnancy?

fuzzyTraps.precise: the rate of growth increases as the pregnancy progresses

chain.text: The mass increases throughout, from 25 g to 3400 g.
The increase in each two month period is much larger than the one before.
The rate of growth increases as the pregnancy progresses.

questions.modelAnswer: The baby grows throughout the pregnancy, with its mass increasing from 25 g at the end of month 3 to 3400 g at the end of month 9. The rate of growth also increases as the pregnancy progresses: the mass increased by 275 g between months 3 and 5, but by 2200 g between months 7 and 9. This means the baby needs an increasing supply of nutrients from the mother as the pregnancy continues.
markPoints: The mass increases throughout the pregnancy, with figures quoted
The rate of growth increases, supported by comparing the gains in different periods
questions.whyMarksLost: Saying only that the baby grows uses the table as a picture rather than as data. The second mark is for spotting that the growth speeds up.

questions.commandDemand: State the effect and explain it using the function of the structure.
questions.stimulus: During pregnancy, the developing baby is surrounded by a bag of fluid inside the uterus.
questions.stem: Predict what would happen if this fluid were not present, and explain the function it serves.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the baby would not be protected from knocks and sudden movements

chain.text: The fluid cushions the developing baby.
It absorbs the force of knocks and sudden movements from outside.
Without it the baby would be more easily injured.

questions.modelAnswer: Without the fluid the developing baby would be far more easily injured. The fluid surrounds and cushions the baby inside the uterus, absorbing the force of any knocks or sudden movements of the mother. It therefore protects the baby from injury while it develops, and also allows it to move freely as it grows.
markPoints: The baby would be more easily injured without the fluid
The fluid cushions and protects the baby from knocks and sudden movements
questions.whyMarksLost: The mechanism, absorbing the force, is what turns 'it protects the baby' into an explanation worth the second mark.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason using the idea of variation between offspring.
questions.stimulus: Two children of the same parents look different from each other and from both of their parents.
questions.stem: Explain why children of the same parents are not identical to each other.

fuzzyTraps.precise: each child inherits a different combination of characteristics from the two parents

chain.text: Each child inherits characteristics from both parents.
A different combination is inherited by each child.
The children show variation and are not identical to each other or to either parent.

questions.modelAnswer: Each child inherits characteristics from both of its parents. However, each child receives a different combination of these characteristics, because the sperm and egg that formed each child were different. This is why the two children show variation and are not identical to each other, and why each resembles but does not exactly match either parent.
markPoints: Characteristics are inherited from both parents
Each child inherits a different combination, so they show variation
questions.whyMarksLost: The word combination carries the answer. Saying only that characteristics are inherited would predict identical children, which is the opposite of what is observed.

questions.commandDemand: State the path in order, naming the parts.
questions.stem: Describe the path taken by water from the soil to a leaf of a plant.

fuzzyTraps.vague: the water goes up the plant
fuzzyTraps.precise: the water travels up through the water carrying tubes in the stem

chain.text: Water is absorbed from the soil by the root hairs.
It passes into the water carrying tubes in the root.
It travels up these tubes through the stem to the leaves.

questions.modelAnswer: Water in the soil is absorbed by the root hairs of the plant. It then passes into the water carrying tubes inside the root. From there the water travels upwards through the water carrying tubes in the stem, and is carried along them into the leaves.
markPoints: Water is absorbed from the soil by the root hairs
It travels up through the water carrying tubes in the stem to the leaves
questions.whyMarksLost: The tubes must be named. Saying the water 'goes up the stem' misses the structure that does the transporting.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason using transpiration and water loss.
questions.stimulus: A plant that has not been watered for several days has drooping, limp leaves.
questions.stem: Explain why the leaves droop.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the plant loses more water by transpiration than it absorbs from the soil
the cells lose water and no longer support the leaf

chain.text: There is no water in the soil for the roots to absorb.
The plant continues to lose water from its leaves by transpiration.
The cells lose water and can no longer support the leaf, so it droops.

questions.modelAnswer: Because the plant has not been watered, there is little water in the soil for the roots to absorb. The plant continues to lose water from its leaves by transpiration, so it loses more water than it takes in. The cells in the leaves therefore lose water and are no longer firm enough to hold the leaf up, so the leaves droop.
markPoints: The plant loses more water by transpiration than it absorbs from the soil
The cells lose water and can no longer support the leaf
questions.whyMarksLost: Transpiration must be named. Without it there is no explanation of where the water went, only that none came in.

questions.commandDemand: State the outcome and explain using the function of the tubes.
questions.stimulus: A ring of bark, containing the food carrying tubes, is removed from all the way around the trunk of a tree. The water carrying tubes deeper inside are left undamaged.
questions.stem: Predict what will happen to the roots of the tree, and explain why.

fuzzyTraps.vague: the tree will die from the cut
fuzzyTraps.precise: food made in the leaves can no longer be transported down to the roots

chain.text: The roots will not receive food and will eventually die.
Food made in the leaves is transported to the rest of the plant through the food carrying tubes.
Removing the ring cuts these tubes all the way round, so food cannot pass below the cut.

questions.modelAnswer: The roots will not receive any food and will eventually die. Food made in the leaves during photosynthesis is transported to the rest of the plant through the food carrying tubes in the bark. Removing a complete ring of bark cuts these tubes all the way around the trunk, so food from the leaves can no longer be carried down past the cut to the roots. Without a supply of food the roots cannot survive.
markPoints: The roots will not receive food and will die
Reason: the food carrying tubes have been cut, so food from the leaves cannot reach the roots
questions.whyMarksLost: The two tube systems do different jobs. Because the water tubes are intact, the leaves still get water; it is the food route downwards that is broken.

questions.commandDemand: Read the results and state what they show, quoting the comparison.
questions.stimulus:
Four leafy shoots were placed in identical tubes of water and the water loss over three hours was measured.

Shoot 1, all leaves left on, still air: 12 ml
Shoot 2, all leaves left on, fan blowing: 21 ml
Shoot 3, half the leaves removed, still air: 7 ml
Shoot 4, all leaves removed, still air: 1 ml
questions.stem: What can you infer from these results about water loss from a plant?

fuzzyTraps.vague: leaves and wind make plants lose water
fuzzyTraps.precise: water is lost mainly from the leaves by transpiration, and moving air increases the rate

chain.text: Comparing Shoots 1, 3 and 4, water loss falls as leaves are removed, so water is lost mainly from the leaves.
Comparing Shoots 1 and 2, where only the air movement differed, the fan increased water loss.
Water is lost from the leaves by transpiration, and moving air increases the rate.

questions.modelAnswer: Water is lost mainly from the leaves by transpiration, and moving air increases the rate of water loss. Comparing Shoots 1, 3 and 4, where only the number of leaves differed, the water loss fell from 12 ml to 7 ml to just 1 ml as leaves were removed, showing that most of the water is lost through the leaves. Comparing Shoot 1 with Shoot 2, where only the air movement differed, the water loss rose from 12 ml to 21 ml, showing that moving air increases the rate of transpiration.
markPoints: Water is lost mainly from the leaves, supported by comparing Shoots 1, 3 and 4
Moving air increases the rate of water loss, supported by comparing Shoots 1 and 2
The process is named as transpiration
questions.whyMarksLost: Shoot 4 still lost 1 ml, which shows a little water is lost elsewhere. Noticing that detail is what separates a careful answer from a rushed one.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason using what the plant needs the water for.
questions.stem: Explain why water is important to a plant.

fuzzyTraps.precise: water is needed for photosynthesis, for support, and to carry mineral salts

chain.text: Water is one of the raw materials needed for photosynthesis.
Water in the cells keeps them firm, which supports the plant and keeps it upright.
Mineral salts absorbed from the soil are transported around the plant dissolved in water.

questions.modelAnswer: Water is one of the raw materials the plant needs for photosynthesis, in which it makes its food. Water inside the cells also keeps them firm, which supports the plant and keeps the stem and leaves upright. In addition, the mineral salts absorbed from the soil are dissolved in water and transported in it to all parts of the plant.
markPoints: Water is needed as a raw material for photosynthesis
Water keeps the cells firm, supporting the plant
Water transports dissolved mineral salts around the plant
questions.whyMarksLost: Three marks means three distinct uses. Most answers give photosynthesis and stop, so the support and transport marks go unclaimed.

questions.commandDemand: Offer a workable method and explain how it reduces water loss.
questions.stimulus: A gardener moves a plant from the ground into a pot. For the next few days the plant wilts in the afternoon sun.
questions.stem: Suggest one thing the gardener could do to help the plant, and explain how it would work.

fuzzyTraps.vague: keep it out of the sun
fuzzyTraps.precise: place it in the shade, which reduces the rate of transpiration

chain.text: Move the plant into the shade during the hottest part of the day.
Less heat energy reduces the rate of transpiration from the leaves.
The plant loses less water, so the roots can replace what is lost and the plant stays firm.

questions.modelAnswer: The gardener could move the plant into the shade during the hottest part of the day. In the shade the leaves receive less heat energy, which reduces the rate of transpiration and so reduces the amount of water lost from the leaves. The roots, which were damaged when the plant was moved, can then absorb enough water to replace what is lost, so the cells stay firm and the plant does not wilt.
markPoints: A workable action such as moving it into the shade or watering it more
Explained as reducing the rate of transpiration so water loss does not exceed absorption
questions.whyMarksLost: The balance between water lost and water absorbed is the mechanism. An answer that only says 'it will not be so hot' has not reached the plant's water balance.

questions.commandDemand: Offer a method that would make the transport visible, and say what would be seen.
questions.stimulus: A teacher wants to show her class the path taken by water inside the stem of a plant.
questions.stem: Suggest how she could do this, and state what the class would observe.

fuzzyTraps.precise: place the cut stem of a white flower in coloured water and leave it for several hours

chain.text: Place the cut stem of a white flower or celery stalk into coloured water.
Leave it for several hours so the water is transported up the stem.
Cut the stem across and see coloured dots where the water carrying tubes are, and coloured petals.

questions.modelAnswer: She could place the cut stem of a white flower, or a stick of celery, into a beaker of coloured water and leave it for several hours. The plant absorbs the coloured water and transports it up the stem. The class would then observe that the petals or the top of the stalk have turned that colour, and if the stem is cut across they would see coloured dots or lines showing exactly where the water carrying tubes are.
markPoints: Method: place a cut stem in coloured water and leave it for several hours
Observation stated: coloured petals, or coloured dots in the cut stem showing the water carrying tubes
questions.whyMarksLost: The observation is half the answer. Describing the setup without saying what would be seen leaves the second mark unclaimed.
